quests.correctSentence: I have finished my homework, so I can relax now.
quests.contrastSentence: I had finished my homework, so I can relax now.
quests.ruleExplanation: Present perfect uses 'have' + past participle for I/you/we/they: I have finished. The result (being able to relax) matters right now, which is the key idea behind this tense.
quests.nativeTip: The subject is 'I', and this connects a past action to the present moment.

quests.correctSentence: She has lost her keys; she can't find them anywhere.
quests.contrastSentence: She have lost her keys; she can't find them anywhere.
quests.ruleExplanation: With he/she/it, present perfect uses 'has': she has lost her keys. The present result, not being able to find them, is what makes this tense the right choice.
quests.nativeTip: The subject 'she' needs the third-person form of 'have'.

quests.correctSentence: — Where's Tom? — He has already left for the airport.
quests.contrastSentence: — Where's Tom? — He have already left for the airport.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'He' takes 'has' in the present perfect: he has left. The relevant result now is that Tom simply isn't here anymore.
quests.nativeTip: Match the subject 'he' with the correct present perfect helper verb.

quests.correctSentence: I have never been to Japan, but I'd love to go.
quests.contrastSentence: I have never be to Japan, but I'd love to go.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Be' has the irregular past participle 'been', used with have/has: have been to Japan. 'Was' would be simple past, which doesn't pair with 'have' this way.
quests.nativeTip: This is the special past participle form of 'be', used after 'have'.

quests.correctSentence: Have you done your homework yet?
quests.contrastSentence: Have you do your homework yet?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Do' has the past participle 'done': have you done it? This differs from the simple past 'did', which wouldn't fit after 'have'.
quests.nativeTip: This is the past participle of 'do', different from its simple past form.

quests.correctSentence: — Has she seen the new movie? — Yes, she's already seen it twice.
quests.contrastSentence: — Has she seen the new movie? — Yes, she's already see it twice.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'See' has the past participle 'seen': has seen, has already seen. This matches the form the question itself already used.
quests.nativeTip: This is the past participle of 'see', matching the question's own form.

quests.conceptTitle: Present Perfect vs Simple Past: Specific Time
quests.grammarRule: Present Perfect vs Simple Past: Specific Time
quests.correctSentence: I went to Paris last year with my family.
quests.contrastSentence: I have gone to Paris last year with my family.
quests.ruleExplanation: A specific past time expression like 'last year' calls for simple past: went last year. Present perfect avoids exact time markers like this.
quests.nativeTip: 'Last year' names a specific, finished point in time.

quests.correctSentence: I have been to Paris; I absolutely loved it there.
quests.contrastSentence: I went to Paris; I absolutely loved it there.
quests.ruleExplanation: Without a specific time marker, present perfect fits general life experience: I have been to Paris. This contrasts with 'went last year' from Question 1, which named an exact time.
quests.nativeTip: No specific time is mentioned here — this is just a general life experience.

quests.conceptTitle: Present Perfect vs Simple Past: Specific Time
quests.grammarRule: Present Perfect vs Simple Past: Specific Time
quests.correctSentence: — Did you finish the report yesterday? — Yes, I finished it yesterday afternoon.
quests.contrastSentence: — Did you finish the report yesterday? — Yes, I have finished it yesterday afternoon.
quests.ruleExplanation: Since 'yesterday afternoon' names an exact time, simple past fits: finished it yesterday. This is the same rule from Question 1, applied to a new example.
quests.nativeTip: 'Yesterday afternoon' is another specific point already in the past.

quests.correctSentence: I've already finished my homework, so I can relax now.
quests.contrastSentence: I've yet finished my homework, so I can relax now.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Already' appears in affirmative sentences to show something is done, often earlier than expected: already finished. 'Yet' is reserved for questions and negatives.
quests.nativeTip: This word emphasizes that something happened sooner than expected, in a positive sentence.

quests.correctSentence: Have you finished your homework yet ?
quests.contrastSentence: Have you finished your homework already ?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Yet' fits at the end of questions asking whether something has happened by now: finished yet? This is the question counterpart to 'already' in Question 1.
quests.nativeTip: This word typically appears at the end of questions, asking if something has happened by now.

quests.correctSentence: — Has he called you back? — Not yet , but I'm sure he will soon.
quests.contrastSentence: — Has he called you back? — Not already , but I'm sure he will soon.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Not yet' is a common short answer meaning something hasn't happened, but is still expected: hasn't called yet. This matches the question form practiced in Question 2.
quests.nativeTip: This short negative answer pairs with the same word used in questions.

quests.correctSentence: I've just arrived; give me a minute to settle in.
quests.contrastSentence: I've yet arrived; give me a minute to settle in.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Just' shows an action was completed very recently: have just arrived. It highlights how little time has passed since the action happened.
quests.nativeTip: This word shows something happened a very short moment ago.

quests.correctSentence: She's just finished her workout, so she's a bit tired.
quests.contrastSentence: She's yet finished her workout, so she's a bit tired.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Just' fits here because the tiredness is a fresh, immediate result: has just finished, so she's tired now.
quests.nativeTip: The tiredness is a direct, immediate result of something that ended only a moment ago.

quests.correctSentence: — Is dinner ready? — Yes, I've just put it on the table; it's still steaming.
quests.contrastSentence: — Is dinner ready? — Yes, I've yet put it on the table; it's still steaming.
quests.ruleExplanation: The detail 'still steaming' points to something extremely recent, matching 'just': have just put it on the table.
quests.nativeTip: The food is still steaming — this happened only moments ago.

quests.correctSentence: Have you ever been to Australia?
quests.contrastSentence: Have you never been to Australia?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Ever' is used in questions asking about experience at any time: have you ever been? 'Never' would only appear in a negative statement, not a question like this.
quests.nativeTip: This word asks about experience at any point in someone's life, in a question.

quests.correctSentence: I've never tried sushi before; I'd like to though.
quests.contrastSentence: I've ever tried sushi before; I'd like to though.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Never' fits statements meaning 'not at any time': have never tried it. This is the statement counterpart to 'ever', which only appears in questions and negatives.
quests.nativeTip: This is a statement, not a question, saying this has not happened at any time.

quests.correctSentence: — Have you ever tried skydiving? — No, I've never done anything that extreme!
quests.contrastSentence: — Have you ever tried skydiving? — No, I've ever done anything that extreme!
quests.ruleExplanation: The answer switches to 'never' because it's now a statement, not a question: have never done anything that extreme, echoing the pattern from Question 2.
quests.nativeTip: The reply is a statement responding to the question's 'ever'.

quests.correctSentence: I've lived here for ten years.
quests.contrastSentence: I've lived here since ten years.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'For' introduces duration that continues into the present with present perfect: have lived for ten years. This is the same 'for' rule from Level 62, now paired with present perfect instead of simple past.
quests.nativeTip: This introduces a length of time, continuing up to now.

quests.correctSentence: I've known her since we were kids.
quests.contrastSentence: I've known her for we were kids.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Since' introduces the starting point of a situation continuing to now: known her since we were kids. This mirrors the 'since' rule from Level 62, now used with present perfect.
quests.nativeTip: This introduces the starting point of the friendship, not its length.

quests.correctSentence: — How long have you worked here? — Since 2015.
quests.contrastSentence: — How long have you worked here? — For 2015.
quests.ruleExplanation: A specific year like 2015 is a starting point, so 'since' fits: since 2015. 'For' would only work with a length of time, like 'for nine years'.
quests.nativeTip: 2015 is a starting point in time, not a length of time.

quests.correctSentence: How long have you been studying English?
quests.contrastSentence: What long have you been studying English?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'How long' is the fixed phrase for asking about duration: how long have you studied? 'What long' isn't a real English question phrase.
quests.nativeTip: This fixed phrase asks specifically about duration.

quests.correctSentence: How long have you known each other?
quests.contrastSentence: How long did you known each other?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'You' takes 'have' in present perfect questions: how long have you known? 'Did' would shift this into simple past, losing the ongoing sense.
quests.nativeTip: The subject 'you' needs the matching present perfect helper verb.

quests.correctSentence: — How long has she been waiting? — She's been waiting for almost an hour.
quests.contrastSentence: — How long has she been waiting? — She's been waiting since almost an hour.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Almost an hour' describes a duration, so 'for' fits: waiting for almost an hour. 'Since' would need a specific starting point instead, like 'since 3 o'clock'.
quests.nativeTip: 'Almost an hour' is a length of time, not a starting point.

quests.correctSentence: I've already finished the report, so I can send it now.
quests.contrastSentence: I've for finished the report, so I can send it now.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Already' fits this affirmative statement about a completed task: have already finished, so it can be sent, reviewing the pattern from Level 104.
quests.nativeTip: This is an affirmative sentence about something finished sooner than expected.

quests.correctSentence: Have you ever visited Italy?
quests.contrastSentence: Have you already visited Italy?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Ever' fits this experience question: have you ever visited? This reviews the pattern from Level 106.
quests.nativeTip: This is a question about experience at any point in life.

quests.correctSentence: — Has the package arrived yet ? — No, not yet.
quests.contrastSentence: — Has the package arrived already ? — No, not yet.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Yet' fits questions asking if something has happened by now: arrived yet? The reply 'not yet' directly confirms this word choice.
quests.nativeTip: This question word is answered with 'not yet' in the reply.

quests.correctSentence: I have worked in marketing for over five years.
quests.contrastSentence: I has worked in marketing for over five years.
quests.ruleExplanation: Present perfect is the natural choice for describing ongoing professional experience in interviews: I have worked for five years, and I'm still working in the field.
quests.nativeTip: This describes professional experience continuing to the present, a common interview pattern.

quests.correctSentence: Have you ever managed a team before?
quests.contrastSentence: Did you ever managed a team before?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Have you ever...?' asks about experience at any point up to now, matching the pattern from Level 106. 'Did' would need a specific past time to sound natural.
quests.nativeTip: This is a life-experience question, matching the subject 'you'.

quests.correctSentence: — Tell me about your experience. — I haven't ever worked in this exact industry, but I'm a fast learner.
quests.contrastSentence: — Tell me about your experience. — I haven't already worked in this exact industry, but I'm a fast learner.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Haven't ever' works the same way as 'never', pairing 'ever' with a negative verb: haven't ever worked here. This closes Stage 6's opening block by combining present perfect with the ever/never distinction from Level 106.
quests.nativeTip: This honest admission uses the negative form, but still needs the question-style partner word.
